project.title: Repair café: what's worth fixing (example walk)

brief.context: It's a repair café in a church hall, once a month on a Saturday. People bring broken lamps and toasters and clothes, and volunteers fix them for free. I suppose I wanted to know why people bother. The volunteers, I think. They give up a whole Saturday, and some of them are quite old. One man spent about an hour on a lamp and then told the owner it wasn't safe to keep, so he didn't fix it in the end. He seemed fine with that.
brief.siteRationale: It's the repair café near me, in a church hall. I've only been twice as a visitor, and I haven't asked anyone yet if I can study it. It won't show me the things that people do with their repairs once they get them home.
brief.processOfInterest: Maybe the repair itself, which takes about an hour for one thing. With the lamp, the volunteer asked the owner about the problem and whether she'd dropped it, and then he plugged it in. I was too far away to follow the rest.
brief.outcomeOfInterest: I don't really know yet. Maybe whether the volunteers fix a thing or not, or the feelings that people have about it afterwards. The volunteer didn't fix the lamp, and he seemed fine with that.
brief.bind: Maybe the volunteers want to fix everything, but they also don't want to waste the owner's time on something cheap. I'm not sure the owners feel that pull too.
brief.sampleRationale: I'm only guessing, but I'd need different kinds of things, like toasters and bikes, and maybe more than one repair café. The bike man only does bikes and two older women do the electrical things, so I'd also need to see the same people with different things.
brief.earlySurprise: I have messy notes from two Saturdays and a short chat with one volunteer. I didn't expect the volunteers to say no to fixing things as often as they did.
brief.startingInterest: I've been to a repair café near me twice, on a Saturday. The volunteers argue about whether a broken thing is worth fixing, and I found that oddly moving. With one toaster, a volunteer said it wasn't worth it because a new one costs about ten pounds, and another said that's exactly the reason to fix it. The woman who brought the toaster just waited for them to decide, and I thought that was a bit strange.
brief.seminalCorpus: I think there's stuff on volunteering? and craft? My supervisor sent me a paper on each. She also sent one on moral economy, but I'm honestly not sure I understood that one.
brief.targetVenue: Whatever my supervisor says, probably a management journal. We haven't talked about it properly yet.
brief.puzzleAnswer: I expected the volunteers to just fix whatever they could. Instead they argue about whether a toaster or a kettle is worth fixing, mostly about money, but at the bike table they just fix the bikes. So why do they argue about toasters but not about bikes? I'm not sure yet that's a proper puzzle.

If you are, my worry is the usual one. Repair cafés vary on host institution (library, church, community center, makerspace), volunteer composition, the items that arrive, city, funding, and the way volunteers judge an item "worth fixing". If you pick two because one looks commercial and one looks communal, or because one is busy and one is quiet, you'll find that they differ. You knew that before collecting any data. You'll observe contrasts in the repairs, and each one sits on top of a dozen other differences, so you can't say which one produced it. Eisenhardt's polar-types logic (1989; Eisenhardt & Graebner, 2007) works only when you match the cases on most dimensions and the focal one varies against that background. Yin's replication logic is stricter: before you collect data, you state your prediction for each case and your reason for it.

A second problem sits underneath this one. You haven't said whether your material is fieldnotes, interviews, or documents, so I can't tell the kind of record you'll end up with. A volunteer saying "we only fix things that teach people something" could be an observed practice, a rehearsed account given to a newcomer, or a line from the café's own flyer. Each reading supports a different claim about "what's worth fixing", and a rehearsed account would change the reading most. Decide which kind of record carries each construct, because a single informant's retrospective account of a single construct is closer to an anecdote than a construct (Yin; Eisenhardt & Graebner on retrospective sensemaking).

Here are three ways forward, and you can pick whichever fits your situation.

First, if you are comparing cafés, write down one dimension of theoretical interest. It might be the criteria for deciding what's worth fixing under volunteer-led versus institution-led governance. Then list the constant dimensions (city, host type, age of the café, item mix) and show that your candidate sites match on each one. If you can't fill in the constant list, treat the design as difference-hunting and rethink the pair.

Second, if you're really after one café, give the extreme, revelatory, or rare-access reason (Yin; Eisenhardt & Graebner). Convenience or depth alone won't carry a single case, and a supervisor or reviewer at a management journal will ask for this reason immediately.

Third, if the design is still open, start from literal replication. Choose two or three cafés, state now your prediction that they'll show the same pattern in their repairs, then add one theoretically specified contrast case. That gives each site a stated job before you've been in the field.

Your puzzle field is blank. The brief gives me a site and the title "what's worth fixing", but no observation from your two visits that surprised you. I'd start there, because the closest published work already answers much of the question as titled. As I remember them (please check the citations, I'm working from memory), Charter and Keiller's survey of Repair Cafés reports that participants cite waste reduction and community far more than saving money. Rosner and Ames, writing on repair and breakdown, show that the decision to fix rests on relationships with objects and with the people who fix them. Moalem and Mosgaard's review of repair initiatives describes the value of repair as assembled from sentimental and ethical reasons, with price mattering little. If your study asks for people's reasons for thinking things are worth fixing and finds attachment, environmental conviction and thrift, it redescribes those three results in a church hall.

An expectation-violating version would start from an observation outside the attachment account's predictions. Examples would be a volunteer declining to touch an object its owner clearly loved, a visitor admitting they'd have binned the item if the café weren't open, or a repair abandoned halfway with everyone content. Did anything like that happen on your two visits? If so, that's your puzzle, and the question becomes the way volunteers and visitors decide worth at the table, and it leaves aside people's later talk about it.

On scope, the brief excludes the people who throw things away, the people who use commercial repair shops or manufacturer schemes, and the volunteers' own reasoning as distinct from the visitors'. You've named the home afterward yourself. In time, you have two visits as a visitor, so the café is a snapshot. I think selection into the café is the exclusion that does the most silent theoretical work. Every visitor in your sample has already decided their object is worth fixing, so you'd study "what's worth fixing" after the visitors have given the answer. The church hall may also supply the moral vocabulary (thrift, stewardship, neighbourliness) that participants then repeat to you.

That connects to the kind of material you'll use, which the brief leaves unstated, and the choice changes what you can see. Fieldnotes from watching triage at the table record decisions as they happen. Interviews will mostly give you rehearsed accounts of someone's reason for coming, which they tell to a stranger. The café's organisers write its signs, posters and sign-in sheets to recruit and reassure, so they show the understanding of worth that the organisers want readers to take. I'd decide this before you write the sample rationale, since you also haven't yet asked whether you can study the café at all.

I see three options. First, write down what you expected to see at the café, then list what from your two visits strained that expectation, and rebuild the question around the strongest strain. Second, keep the site and narrow the question to the decisions volunteers and visitors make at the table (the objects they accept, refuse or abandon), using observation with repeated visits, and treat the home as a later study. Third, if you want to keep the broader question, accept as a scope condition that you're studying worth only among people already committed to repair, and say so in the brief. Whichever you choose, talk to your supervisor about the management journal soon. You could cast the same observations as valuation, volunteer organizing or hybrid community-market forms, and each casing points to a different literature, and you'd need to read it first.

If you're asking about the reasons people bring broken things to a repair café, or about the finding that people value repair for sustainability and sentimental reasons, I'd expect the literature to answer it already, and your study would redescribe a known regularity in a church hall. An expectation-violating version would ask about the reasons people decline to repair items that are cheap and fixable, or about the differences between the items the volunteers judge worth fixing and the items visitors judge worth fixing. Your brief shows no data chunks, and you haven't said whether your material is fieldnotes from your two visits, things volunteers told you, or something the café produced for its own purposes, like a sign-in sheet or a poster of rules. I can't draw two anomalies from outside your retrieval set because I can't see a retrieval set, and I won't cite chunk IDs you haven't given me. I can name two places to look once material exists, and name the expectation each would violate if it showed up.

The first candidate is any occasion at the bike table on which people did argue about whether a repair was worth it, or any toaster or kettle that a volunteer fixed without a word. Your puzzle treats object type as the thing that predicts argument. A single exception would strain that expectation and point toward something else doing the sorting, such as the people standing at the table, the person bringing the object in, or the busyness of the afternoon. The second candidate is any moment in which a volunteer invokes "money" although the people present aren't paying anything. Volunteers give their time free, and visitors presumably pay little or no money. If your volunteers argue about cost anyway, the thing at risk is your expectation that they're running a cost-benefit calculation. The argument might then be about the worth of the object, about the standard for proper repair, or about volunteers showing skill to each other. Both candidates are conditional. I'm naming them because they sit at the edges of your stated contrast, and I can't confirm that either appears in your collected material.

On provenance, your claim that volunteers "argue about whether a toaster or a kettle is worth fixing" could rest on three different kinds of record. If you overheard an argument, you have an observation. If a volunteer described the arguments to you, you have a rehearsed account, and a volunteer telling a visitor "we always debate the toasters" may be performing the café's self-image. If a poster or a policy sheet says toasters are judged case by case, the setting produced that for its own reasons and for readers other than you. Each reading changes what your puzzle is a puzzle about.

This matters because you've stated your expectation ("I expected the volunteers to just fix whatever they could") clearly enough that evidence can defeat it, and I'd keep it. A management reviewer will ask about the basis of the contrast, though, and two visits as a visitor without permission to study the site are a thin base for any of the three record types. If the toaster-versus-bike contrast comes from an impression, you can't yet tell whether you've found an anomaly or a quirk of your two visits. Two years from now, a design that doesn't separate observed from recounted material will leave you unable to say which of your findings the volunteers' self-presentation produced.

You have three choices. You could write up your two visits as fieldnotes this week, marking each line as seen, told to you, or printed in the hall, and load that as your first material so I can nominate anomalies with real chunk citations. You could ask the organizers for permission to attend as a researcher and plan a third visit aimed at the bike table's exceptions and the invocations of money. Or you could keep the puzzle as it stands and name the contrast as a working hunch, with the scope condition that you haven't yet established which kind of record supports it. The first choice is the quickest, and I'd start there.

events.text: I can see that your ledger lists 15 challenges and 0 adjudications, but no challenge text and no data chunks came through with this stage, so I can't restate each one or mark which anomaly candidate it touches. That count is the first concern. Your one candidate, the contrast between arguments over toasters and kettles and the absence of arguments at the bike table, is currently carried by an unanswered stack of objections. Until you answer, concede, or park each one with a stated reason, that candidate is a hypothesis, and you'd need to present it with the surviving objections attached. Abductive work depends on a community of inquiry testing your casing (Tavory & Timmermans 2014). Fifteen unanswered challenges mean the testing has happened and you haven't yet answered it. You have three options. You could paste the 15 here and write one line against each (answered, conceded, or still open with your reason), which takes an hour or so. You could merge duplicates first, since several are probably the same objection in different words, and adjudicate the remainder. Or you could leave them open and label the toaster-versus-bike contrast as a hypothesis in every note and draft until they're resolved.

Your puzzle statement doesn't name the kind of record it comes from. You've been twice as a visitor, so I can't tell whether "they argue about whether a toaster or a kettle is worth fixing, mostly about money" comes from your own watching, from a volunteer's telling, or from your own piecing together afterwards. The reading that changes most is "mostly about money". If a volunteer said it to you, it's a rehearsed account of the reasons they decline some repairs, and the money explanation is then the members' own casing, and you haven't observed it as a mechanism. The same question applies to "at the bike table they just fix the bikes". Silence at the bike table could mean agreement, or it could mean a different decision rule that you didn't see because the argument happened at intake. The form of your own sentence also tells me something. "I expected the volunteers to just fix whatever they could" is your expectation. A surprise needs the expectation of some community of inquiry, and you haven't yet said whose it is. Your management-journal target will want that named. You could write a short note sorting each claim in your puzzle into watched, told, or inferred, and check the share of the contrast that survives. You could name the literature whose expectation you're violating (valuation of low-cost goods, repair as craft, or volunteer work are three candidates) and state the prediction that literature makes for toasters and bikes. Or you could state in one sentence what you currently expect to find at a third visit, so that the visit can contradict you.

Your site rationale says you haven't asked anyone if you can study the café, and two visits as a visitor is the whole basis of the anomaly. With that base, I can't see a way for you to tell the pattern from the accident of two particular Saturdays. The bike table may have had one experienced volunteer on those days, or the toaster arguments may have come from one pair of people. Abductive analysis gets its pressure from variation within the case, the situations where the pattern applies, bends and breaks (A10), and two visits give you too little of that to test any casing. Money is one casing. Others would be that bikes are owned by people who ride them and so arrive already worth fixing, or that the bike table has a different division of labor. Each of those would be visible only with more time at the site. You could ask the organizers for permission to attend as a researcher over several sessions and treat your current puzzle as a pilot observation. You could write up the two visits now as fieldnotes and mark the casings that remain inseparable for now. Or you could decide the café isn't the right site and list your requirements for a different one. Whichever you choose, settle your data type before the next visit, because the choice between observing, interviewing, and collecting the café's own documents decides whether any of these casings become distinguishable.

I can see that your ledger holds 168 events, 15 challenges and 0 adjudications. I can't see the text of those 15 challenges, and no data chunks are selected, so I can't list each objection with the anomaly candidates it touches. I won't guess at them. What I can say is that your anomaly (volunteers argue about toasters and kettles, mostly about money, while at the bike table they just fix bikes) is firming up while every objection sits unanswered. A candidate with unresolved challenges against it is a hypothesis, not a finding. At this stage, the toaster-versus-bike contrast needs to be written down as a hypothesis with the surviving objections attached, even if some of those objections turn out to be weak.

The second concern is the kind of record you're working from. You've been twice as a visitor and haven't asked anyone for access. So the material behind the contrast is probably your memory or notes of two afternoons. Was the toaster argument something you watched happen, something a volunteer described to you, or something the café says about itself on a poster or a sign-in sheet? Those are three different records. If volunteers told you "we argue about money", that's a rehearsed account offered to a newcomer, and your money reading would change a great deal. It would then be a story the café tells about itself, and the argument at the table might not match it. The form of whatever you have also tells you something. A line in your notes that says "they argue about money" was written by you, for you, after the fact, and has already compressed the sequence of who said what and in what order.

This matters for the process question you're asking. A process account of how a verdict on "worth fixing" gets reached needs events: who brought the item, who looked at it, what was said, when the argument started and stopped. Two visits can't give you the sequence, and retrospective impressions tend to rationalize it (Langley et al., 2013). The bike table may also differ in something other than the item, such as who staffs it, whether the owner is standing there, or whether the repair is already agreed before anyone speaks. Each of those is a rival reading of your contrast, and I'd expect several of your 15 open challenges to point at them.

I see three options. First, paste the 15 challenges here and we adjudicate them together. For each, write the strongest form, name the anomaly candidate it touches, and mark it answered, open, or unanswerable with your current material. Second, go back through what you have from the two visits and tag each passage as observed, recounted, or produced by the café for its own purposes. Then check which of your claims about money survive if only the observed passages count. Third, if you accept that two visits can't support a finding, state the contrast as a hypothesis in your next draft with the open objections listed beside it, and treat asking the organizers for access as the next step. Real-time observation across several sessions, plus any posted rules or logs, would let you see the sequence and tell you whether toasters and bikes really differ.

I have no data chunks at this stage, so I can't cite a passage, and I'm reading your brief as the only record in front of me. In your puzzle, you say the volunteers "argue about whether a toaster or a kettle is worth fixing, mostly about money, but at the bike table they just fix the bikes." In your Site answer, you say you've been twice as a visitor and haven't asked anyone anything. The honest version of the puzzle is therefore: on two visits, I noticed some argument over small electricals and, as far as I noticed, none at the bike table. Three parts of that sentence are uncorroborated. "Mostly about money" has no stated source. You haven't said whether you overheard an argument or a volunteer told you about one. "The bike man only does bikes and two older women do the electrical things" comes from two visits and possibly one conversation. "They just fix the bikes" rests on the small amount you saw at one table.

The provenance matters because the three kinds of record support different readings. If you overheard a volunteer weigh a kettle's repair cost against a new one, you have an observation. If a volunteer told you "we always argue about money," you have a rehearsed account, which shows the way people describe the café and says little about the way volunteers make decisions. If a sign or price list says "we don't repair items under £10," the setting produced it for visitors, and it shows the activity the café wants visitors to see. Your "mostly about money" reads differently under each. You haven't yet named, in your brief, the kind of record you have.

Your own material also contains a rival explanation that the puzzle doesn't name. The bike man works alone, and two women share the electricals. Arguments need at least two people, so the bike table may be quiet because only one person is deciding. Item value, safety risk with mains electricity, and the cost of a replacement toaster against a replacement bike are further rivals. Right now person and object type are the same variable, so you couldn't separate them in any pattern you saw.

At review this matters a great deal. A reviewer in a management journal will read a two-visit puzzle with an unnamed informant source as an anecdote (Yin's construct-validity test asks for several sources converging on the same construct). Eisenhardt and Graebner's concern about retrospective accounts applies the moment a volunteer's explanation of "money" becomes your explanation. If you carry the confident version into a proposal, you could spend two years explaining a contrast that came from a staffing arrangement. You've already noticed the fix when you wrote that you'd need to see the same people with different things. That is the right instinct, because it keeps the person constant and varies the object. Access is the other gap: you haven't yet asked anyone whether you can study the café, and observation of repair decisions depends on that answer.

I see three ways to go. First, keep the puzzle as a pilot observation and mark it that way. Write "on two visits, one table appeared quiet, not yet corroborated," and at your next visit keep separate field-note columns for your own observations, the statements people made to you (with the speaker), and the signs and notes in the hall. That costs one morning and tells you which kind of record you have. Second, plan the data that would support the confident claim. That means several sessions with each argument logged by item, the speaker and the words used, interviews with the bike man, both electrical volunteers and the organizer, and any repair log or sign the café keeps. Ask the organizer for access before you design anything else. Third, state a prediction in advance and choose a second site to test it. If the argument depends on the number of fixers, a café where one person handles electricals and several handle bikes should reverse your pattern. If it depends on the item's value, the pattern should stay the same. Write down your expected outcome and your reasons before you collect anything, and raise them with your supervisor, since the venue conversation will shape the number of sites you need.

events.text:
I can't pull out the excerpts your open challenges point at, because you haven't attached any data chunks at this stage, and the ledger shows 21 challenges with 0 adjudications. So I'm not citing any chunk IDs. The one pair of observations I can work from is in your puzzle statement, and I suspect it's also the material that comes up in the challenges: people argue about whether a toaster or a kettle is worth fixing, and at the bike table the bike man just fixes bikes.

I'd like to describe those two observations without the word "worth". At the electrical table, an object arrives and people talk about money before they open it up. At the bike table, an object arrives and the work starts. Your puzzle treats the second as an absence of the first, as if deliberating about worth were the default and the bike table were the exception. Some other concept might fit better. Perhaps the bike man answers the question of whether to repair before the object reaches the table, through his trade, the price of a new bike, or his way of taking a bike in. Perhaps two people at the electrical table ask the question because they have different views of safety or cost and are standing at one object. You also mention that the bike man only does bikes and two older women do the electrical things. That makes the contrast a difference between people and trades as much as between objects, and you absorb that difference into the category "worth of the object" without deciding to.

Your brief also doesn't name the kind of record you have. You've been twice as a visitor and haven't asked anyone for access, so I'd guess your material is memory of your own observations, or of the volunteers' remarks to you. Those are different records. If you overheard "mostly about money" between volunteers, it's an observation. If a volunteer told you it in answer to your question, it may be a rehearsed account the volunteers offer a visitor, and money could be the reason that's easy to say to a stranger. That reading would change the most. The passage's own form matters too: a remark to you, your own note afterwards, and a sign on the wall each come from different people for different readers.

This matters because, in process terms (Langley 1999), your elementary unit is the event, and you haven't yet defined one. Is an argument an event? Is the arrival of a toaster? Is it an event when someone wheels a bike in and the bike man works on it without comment? Until you decide, "arguing about worth" will take in whatever happens near a toaster. Langley's point about retrospective accounts (Langley et al. 2013) applies as well. Accounts given after the fact tidy the sequence in light of the outcome, so a decision that looks like a money argument in hindsight may have begun as something else. If 21 challenges stay unadjudicated into the main study, you'll have absorbed every residual observation into the category, and you won't be able to name the ones you trimmed.

I see three options. First, spend a sitting adjudicating the open challenges. For each one that concerns the toaster and bike contrast, write down in plain words your observation or the remark you heard, with no mention of worth, and then accept, revise or reject the challenge. Second, before any further analysis, label each passage you have as observed, recounted to you, or produced by the café itself, and note the date and the people present. You'll then see which readings survive if volunteers turn out to have rehearsed some. Third, if you ask the organisers for access, plan your next visit around single items rather than themes. Follow a toaster and a bike from arrival to outcome at both tables, noting the point where someone raises the question of repairing, that person's role, and whether anyone raises it at all. You could also stay with "worth" as a loose pilot-stage label, if you write down that you're doing so and the differences the label might hide.
